claim: Variants are observed at approximately 3.1% of the measurable sites in the reference human genome (GRCh38).
source: We observe variants at ~3.1% of the measurable sites in the reference human genome (GRCh38).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A which shows this percentage visually.

claim: A measurable site is one at which it is possible to detect variation with current sequencing technologies, currently approximately 2.9 Gb out of 3.1 Gb in the human genome.
source: A measurable site is one at which it is possible to detect variation with current sequencing technologies (currently approximately 2.9 Gb out of 3.1 Gb in the human genome; ).
evidence: The claim defines what constitutes a measurable site and provides specific measurements based on current sequencing technology capabilities.

claim: 85% of variants fall into just eight codes out of the 242 that are possible.
source: The distribution of codes is heavily concentrated, with 85% of variants falling into just eight codes out of the 242 that are possible (35–1: three frequency categories in each of five regional groupings, subtracting the code 'UUUUU' as each variant has been observed by definition).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on analysis of the 1000 Genomes dataset.

claim: The top four most abundant codes represent rare variants that are localized in a single region.
source: Of the top eight codes, the top four codes represent rare variants that are localized in a single region.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by the data visualization in Figure 3.

claim: The fifth most abundant code, 'RuuuR', represents rare variants found in Africa and the Admixed Americas.
source: The fifth most abundant code, 'RuuuR', represents rare variants found in Africa and the Admixed Americas (which includes African American individuals, for example).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on the geographic distribution coding scheme applied to the data.

claim: The seventh most abundant code is 'CCCCC' or 'globally common variants.'
source: The seventh code is 'CCCCC' or 'globally common variants.'
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by Figure 3B.

claim: When a variant is found to be common (>5% allele frequency) in one population, the modal pattern (37.3%) is that it is common across the five regions ('CCCCC').
source: Instead, when a variant is found to be common (>5% allele frequency) in one population, the modal pattern (37.3%) is that it is common across the five regions ('CCCCC').
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 63% of variants common in at least one region are also globally widespread, in the sense of being found across all five regions.
source: Further, 63% of variants common in at least one region are also globally widespread, in the sense of being found across all five regions.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: This number rises to 82% for variants common in at least one region outside of Africa.
source: This number rises to 82% for variants common in at least one region outside of Africa (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Removing singletons reduces the absolute number of variants observed by 48.2% (91,784,637 vs. 44,290,364).
source: Removing singletons reduces the absolute number of variants observed by 48.2% (91,784,637 vs. 44,290,364).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by comparison of Figure 3B and Figure 3C.

claim: At 96.6% of variants (80,068,013/82,919,198), the minor allele is also the derived allele.
source: At 96.6% of variants (80,068,013/82,919,198), the minor allele is also the derived allele.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Localized rare variants (such as 'Ruuuu' or 'uuuRu') are mostly young mutations that have not had time to spread geographically.
source: Thus, we interpret the localized rare variants (such as 'Ruuuu' or 'uuuRu') as mostly young mutations that have not had time to spread geographically.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on population genetics principles and is supported by citations to relevant literature (Mathieson and McVean, 2014; Kiezun et al., 2013; Kimura and Ohta, 1973; Albers and McVean, 2020).

claim: The code 'CCCCC' (globally common variants) likely comprises mostly older variants that arose in Africa and were spread globally during the Out-of-Africa migration and other dispersal events.
source: The code 'CCCCC' (globally common variants), likely comprises mostly older variants that arose in Africa and were spread globally during the Out-of-Africa migration and other dispersal events (see Box 2).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on population genetics theory and human evolutionary history.

claim: The appearance of rare variants shared between two or more regions (codes with two 'R's and three 'u's, such as 'uuRRu' or 'RRuuu') is likely the signature of recent gene flow between those regions.
source: The appearance of rare variants shared between two or more regions (codes with two 'R's and three 'u's, such as 'uuRRu' or 'RRuuu') is likely the signature of recent gene flow between those regions (Box 2; Platt et al., 2019; Mathieson and McVean, 2014; Gutenkunst et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The abundant 'RuuuR' and 'uRuuR' codes likely represent young variants that are shared between the Admixed Americas and Africa ('RuuuR') or Europe ('uRuuR') because of the population movements during the last 500 years that began with European colonization of the Americas and the subsequent slave trade from Africa.
source: In particular, the abundant 'RuuuR' and 'uRuuR' codes likely represent young variants that are shared between the Admixed Americas and Africa ('RuuuR') or Europe ('uRuuR') because of the population movements during the last 500 years that began with European colonization of the Americas and the subsequent slave trade from Africa.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on known historical events and their genetic consequences.

claim: The 10th most abundant code ('CuuuR') is interpreted as mostly variants that were lost in the Out-of-Africa bottleneck and subsequently carried to the Americas by African ancestors.
source: We interpret the 10th most abundant code ('CuuuR', Figure 3B) as mostly variants that were lost in the Out-of-Africa bottleneck and subsequently carried to the Americas by African ancestors.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on population genetics theory regarding bottleneck effects.

claim: There is a relative absence of variants that are common in only one region outside of Africa and absent across all others (e.g. 'uCuuu', 'uuCuu', 'uuuCu', 'uuuuC').
source: There is a relative absence of variants that are common in only one region outside of Africa and absent across all others (e.g. 'uCuuu', 'uuCuu', 'uuuCu', 'uuuuC').
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by the data visualization in Figure 3.

claim: These patterns are consistent with human populations having not diverged deeply, in the sense that there has not been sufficient time for genetic drift to greatly shift allele frequencies among them.
source: These patterns are consistent with human populations having not diverged deeply, in the sense that there has not been sufficient time for genetic drift to greatly shift allele frequencies among them (Box 2).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on population genetics theory and is supported by Box 2.

claim: Overall, these results reflect a timescale of divergence consistent with the Recent-African-Origin model of human evolution as well as subsequent gene flow among regions.
source: Overall, these results reflect a timescale of divergence consistent with the Recent-African-Origin model of human evolution as well as subsequent gene flow among regions (Cann et al., 1987; Stringer and Andrews, 1988; Thomson et al., 2000; Ramachandran et al., 2005; Pickrell and Reich, 2014).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by citations to relevant literature on human evolution.

claim: The variants that differ between pairs of individuals are typically globally widespread (i.e. codes with no 'u's, with proportions out of the total S varying from 54% to 76% for the pairs in Figure 4).
source: We see that the variants that differ between each pair of individuals are typically globally widespread (i.e. codes with no 'u's, with proportions out of the total S varying from 54% to 76% for the pairs in Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Pairs of individuals mostly differ because one of them carries a common variant that the other does not; and common variants in any single location are often common throughout the world.
source: Instead, pairs of individuals mostly differ because one of them carries a common variant that the other does not; and as Figure 3 already showed, common variants in any single location are often common throughout the world (also see Figure 6 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the data presented in multiple figures.

claim: The two Yoruba individuals have more pairwise SNVs (S = 4,897,091) than the French/French (S = 3,525,519) and Han/Han (S = 3,358,497) pairs.
source: For example, the two Yoruba individuals have more pairwise SNVs (S = 4,897,091) than the French/French (S = 3,525,519) and Han/Han (S = 3,358,497) pairs.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Higher diversity in Africa is typically interpreted in terms of founder effects reducing diversity outside of Africa.
source: One also observes evidence for higher diversity in Africa, which is typically interpreted in terms of founder effects reducing diversity outside of Africa (Cann et al., 1987; Harpending and Eller, 2000; Harpending and Rogers, 2000; Ramachandran et al., 2005; Prugnolle et al., 2005), although other models, especially ones including substantial subsequent admixture, can also produce this pattern (DeGiorgio et al., 2009; Pickrell and Reich, 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The process of discovering and selecting target sites for genotyping arrays typically enriches the probe sets toward common variants.
source: The process of discovering and selecting these target sites typically enriches the probe sets toward common variants (Clark et al., 2005), underrepresents geographically localized variants (Albrechtsen et al., 2010; Lachance and Tishkoff, 2013), and can affect genotype imputation and genetic risk prediction (Howie et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The process of discovering and selecting target sites for genotyping arrays underrepresents geographically localized variants.
source: The process of discovering and selecting these target sites typically enriches the probe sets toward common variants (Clark et al., 2005), underrepresents geographically localized variants (Albrechtsen et al., 2010; Lachance and Tishkoff, 2013), and can affect genotype imputation and genetic risk prediction (Howie et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: A large fraction of the variants on genotyping arrays are globally common, in stark contrast with the SNVs identified by whole-genome sequencing.
source: In stark contrast with the SNVs identified by whole-genome sequencing (Figure 3B), a large fraction of the variants on genotyping arrays are globally common.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by comparison of Figure 3B and Figure 5.

claim: The Affy6, Human Origins, and OmniExpress arrays were designed using polymorphisms ascertained from a smaller number of sequenced individuals, and primarily capture more common variants due to this ascertainment.
source: This is especially true for the Affy6, Human Origins, and OmniExpress arrays, which were designed using polymorphisms ascertained from a smaller number of sequenced individuals, and primarily capture more common variants due to this ascertainment.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The MEGA array was uniquely designed to capture rare variation in undersampled continental groups, including African ancestries.
source: The MEGA array was uniquely designed to capture rare variation in undersampled continental groups, including African ancestries (Bien et al., 2016; Bien et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The MEGA array design improved African and African American imputation accuracy, leading to greater power to map population-specific disease risk.
source: Wojcik et al., 2019 found that this design improved African and African American imputation accuracy, leading to greater power to map population-specific disease risk.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by a citation to Wojcik et al., 2019.

claim: The majority of variants are seen to be rare and geographically localized (1 'R', and the remainder 'u's) when using a 26-digit encoding for the 1KGP variants.
source: Doing so with the set of ~92 million variants found in the 1KGP project (Figure 6), we find a consistent pattern with Figure 3B, in that the majority of variants are seen to be rare and geographically localized (1 'R', and the remainder 'u's), and when a variant is common in any one population, it is typically common across the full set of populations (Figure 6, pattern with all 'C's).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: When a variant is common in any one population, it is typically common across the full set of populations when using a 26-digit encoding.
source: Doing so with the set of ~92 million variants found in the 1KGP project (Figure 6), we find a consistent pattern with Figure 3B, in that the majority of variants are seen to be rare and geographically localized (1 'R', and the remainder 'u's), and when a variant is common in any one population, it is typically common across the full set of populations (Figure 6, pattern with all 'C's).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The average sample size across all geographic regions is approximately 500 individuals (AFR: 504, EUR: 404, SAS: 489, EAS: 504, AMR: 603).
source: The average sample size across all of our geographic regions is approximately 500 individuals (AFR: 504, EUR: 404, SAS: 489, EAS: 504, AMR: 603).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and provides specific sample sizes for each region.

claim: Assuming regions are internally well-mixed, there is approximately 80% power to detect alleles with a frequency of approximately 0.2% in a region.
source: Assuming regions are internally well-mixed, we have ~80% power to detect alleles with a frequency of ~0.2% in a region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In large samples, we should observe more rare variant sharing.
source: An implication is that in large samples, we should observe more rare variant sharing.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on statistical power considerations.

claim: The GeoVar plot is a visualization of the joint SFS for the sample, rather than for the complete population.
source: In general, one must keep in mind that the GeoVar plot is a visualization of the joint SFS for the sample, rather than for the complete population.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a caveat about the interpretation of the visualization.

claim: The 1KGP filtered for individuals of a single ethnicity within each locale.
source: In particular, the 1KGP filtered for individuals of a single ethnicity within each locale.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a description of the 1KGP study design.

claim: In our current cosmopolitan world, the genetic diversity in any location or broad-based sampling project will be considerably higher than implied by the geographic groupings used in this study.
source: However, in our current cosmopolitan world, the genetic diversity in any location or broad-based sampling project will be considerably higher than implied by the geographic groupings above.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a caveat about the interpretation of the results.

claim: The UK Biobank, while predominantly of European ancestry, has representation of individuals with ancestry from each of the five regions used in this study.
source: For example, the UK Biobank, while predominantly of European ancestry, has representation of individuals with ancestry from each of the five regions used here (Bycroft et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by a citation to Bycroft et al., 2018.

claim: The well-established introgression of archaic hominids (e.g. Neandertals, Denisovans) into modern human populations is not apparent in the GeoVar plots produced.
source: The well-established introgression of archaic hominids (e.g. Neandertals, Denisovans) into modern human populations (Wolf and Akey, 2018) is not apparent in the GeoVar plots we produced.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by a citation to Wolf and Akey, 2018.

claim: The clearest signal of archaic introgression will come from sites where archaic hominids differed from modern humans, and these sites are only a very small fraction of variants found in humans today.
source: The clearest signal of archaic introgression will come from sites where archaic hominids differed from modern humans, and we expect that these sites are only a very small fraction of variants found in humans today.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as an explanation for why archaic introgression is not apparent in the GeoVar plots.

claim: The average human–Neandertal and human–Denisovan sequence divergence are both less than 0.16%.
source: The average human–Neandertal and human–Denisovan sequence divergence are both less than 0.16% (using observations from Prüfer et al., 2014), and a recent study estimates that there are fewer than 70 Mb (2.3% of the genome) of Neanderthal introgressed segments per individual for all individuals in the 1KGP (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by citations to Prüfer et al., 2014 and Chen et al., 2020.

claim: There are fewer than 70 Mb (2.3% of the genome) of Neanderthal introgressed segments per individual for all individuals in the 1KGP.
source: The average human–Neandertal and human–Denisovan sequence divergence are both less than 0.16% (using observations from Prüfer et al., 2014), and a recent study estimates that there are fewer than 70 Mb (2.3% of the genome) of Neanderthal introgressed segments per individual for all individuals in the 1KGP (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2020.

claim: Archaic introgression events are believed to be old: >30,000 years ago, allowing time for substantial genetic drift and admixture among human populations.
source: Archaic introgression events are believed to be old: >30,000 years ago, allowing time for substantial genetic drift and admixture among human populations (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2020.

claim: Negative selection and, in some cases, strong positive selection have shaped the patterns of introgressed SNVs.
source: Negative selection (Harris and Nielsen, 2016; Juric et al., 2016) and, in some cases, strong positive selection Racimo et al., 2015 have also shaped the patterns of introgressed SNVs.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Low levels of archaic introgression are not expected to create a striking visual deviation in GeoVar plots from the background patterns of a Recent African Origin model with subsequent migration.
source: For these reasons, we expect low levels of archaic introgression not to create a striking visual deviation in our GeoVar plots from the background patterns of a Recent African Origin model with subsequent migration (Box 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as an inference based on the characteristics of archaic introgression.

claim: Many common variant associations replicate across populations.
source: Indeed, many common variant associations replicate across populations (Marigorta and Navarro, 2013; though see Martin et al., 2017; Mostafavi et al., 2020 for complications).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Rare variants are likely to be geographically restricted.
source: As our work here emphasizes, rare variants are likely to be geographically restricted, and so one can expect the rare variants found in one population will not be useful for explaining trait variation in other populations, although they may identify relevant biological pathways that are shared across populations.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as an inference based on the data presented.

claim: Rare variants found in one population will not be useful for explaining trait variation in other populations, although they may identify relevant biological pathways that are shared across populations.
source: As our work here emphasizes, rare variants are likely to be geographically restricted, and so one can expect the rare variants found in one population will not be useful for explaining trait variation in other populations, although they may identify relevant biological pathways that are shared across populations.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as an inference based on the data presented.

claim: In studies with sample sizes similar to or smaller than the 1KGP, nearly all SNVs arise from single mutation events.
source: We note that in studies with sample sizes similar to or smaller than the 1KGP, nearly all SNVs arise from single mutation events.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a general observation about SNVs.

claim: For highly mutable loci, independently derived alleles will be distributed in disjoint regions of the world due to multiple mutational origins.
source: In contrast, for highly mutable loci we expect independently derived alleles will be distributed in disjoint regions of the world due to multiple mutational origins (Ralph and Coop, 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by a citation to Ralph and Coop, 2010.

claim: Recent advances in the inference of genome-wide tree sequences and allele ages allow for quantitative summaries of ancestral lineage sharing.
source: Recent advances in the inference of genome-wide tree sequences (Kelleher et al., 2019; Speidel et al., 2019) and allele ages (Albers and McVean, 2020) allow for quantitative summaries of ancestral lineage sharing.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Ancestral lineage sharing quantities have a close relationship to the multi-population SFS properties studied in this work, yet are more fundamental in a sense and less subject to the stochasticity of the mutation process.
source: Such quantities have a close relationship to the multi-population SFS properties that are studied here, yet are more fundamental in a sense and less subject to the stochasticity of the mutation process.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a comparison between different approaches.

claim: The conceptual simplicity of visualizing allele frequency patterns may be an advantage in educational settings.
source: That said, the conceptual simplicity of visualizing allele frequency patterns may be an advantage in educational settings.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a consideration for the approach presented.

claim: The 1000 Genomes Project samples were grouped into five geographical ancestry groups: African (AFR), European (EUR), South Asian (SAS), East Asian (EAS), and Admixed American (AMR).
source: First, we follow the 1KGP study in grouping the samples from the 26 populations into five geographical ancestry groups: African (AFR), European (EUR), South Asian (SAS), East Asian (EAS), and Admixed American (AMR) (Figure 2A, Box 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by Figure 2A.

claim: A threshold of 5% frequency was used to distinguish between 'rare' and 'common' alleles.
source: To distinguish between 'rare' and 'common' alleles, we used a threshold of 5% frequency.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as part of the methodology.

claim: The 1000 Genomes Project contains approximately 92 million biallelic SNVs.
source: Using the encoding scheme just described, we generated geographic distribution codes for all ~92 million biallelic SNVs in the 1000 Genomes dataset and display their relative proportions (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by Figure 3.

claim: 242 possible geographic distribution codes exist (3^5 - 1).
source: The distribution of codes is heavily concentrated, with 85% of variants falling into just eight codes out of the 242 that are possible (35–1: three frequency categories in each of five regional groupings, subtracting the code 'UUUUU' as each variant has been observed by definition).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text with an explanation of how the number is calculated.

claim: Singleton variants are the most abundant type of variant in human genetic data.
source: Singleton variants—alleles found in a single individual—are the most abundant type of variant in human genetic data and are necessarily found in just one geographic region.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a general observation about human genetic data.

claim: Singleton variants are necessarily found in just one geographic region.
source: Singleton variants—alleles found in a single individual—are the most abundant type of variant in human genetic data and are necessarily found in just one geographic region.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a logical consequence of the definition of singleton variants.

claim: The SGDP sampled 300 individuals from 142 diverse populations.
source: The SGDP sampled 300 individuals from 142 diverse populations.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a description of the SGDP dataset.

claim: Rare variants are not often carried by either individual in a pair precisely because rare variants are rare.
source: However, precisely because rare variants are rare, they are not often carried by either individual in a pair.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as an explanation for the observed patterns.

claim: The Omni2.5Exome and MEGA arrays exhibit many more rare variants compared to the Affy6, Human Origins, and OmniExpress arrays.
source: The Omni2.5Exome and MEGA arrays in contrast exhibit many more rare variants.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In both the Omni2.5Exome and MEGA arrays, the second and third most abundant codes are 'CuuuR' and 'RuuuR' variants.
source: In both these arrays, the second and third most abundant codes are 'CuuuR' and 'RuuuR' variants.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by data shown in Figure 5.
